title: Localization vs. Standardization: Building a Payment Strategy for Southeast Asia Expansion
summary: Balance payment localization and standardization for SEA expansion without building separate setups for each market.
body_markdown:
Southeast Asia's e-commerce payments are moving to digital methods quickly, yet customers in each country still


**pay in different ways** . Any payment strategy for Southeast Asia expansion has to start from both facts, that the region is ready to


**pay online** , and each market does so through its own


**mix of payment methods** .


For a business operating in several SEA markets, the challenge is


**adapting payment acceptance to local customers** without building a separate payment operation for every country. A regional payment strategy therefore has to balance two layers:


- **Localization:** Supporting the payment methods and payment experience that customers expect in each market


- **Standardization:** Keeping the integration, operations, and reporting behind those payments consistent across markets


The payment experience your customers expect varies in each market, while the infrastructure should stay as standardized as possible. Getting that split right decides how much local demand your checkout converts in each country, and how much extra work each new market adds for your engineering and finance teams.


**Here is what this article covers:**


- Why payment acceptance has to be localized across Southeast Asia, from national payment rails to refund and settlement rules


- Why the integration, operations, and reporting underneath should stay standardized as you add markets


- What over-standardizing and over-localizing each cost a regional business


- Five areas to evaluate before choosing or redesigning your regional payment infrastructure


- How Xendit combines localized payment acceptance with standardized payment operations


## **Localization: Supporting local payment methods in each Southeast Asian market**


Payment preferences in Southeast Asia follow the banking and payment systems each country has developed. Three


**factors** make


**payment localization** necessary for businesses selling across the region:


### **Each market has its own payment preferences and infrastructure**


Digital payments are quickly becoming the standard way to pay online in Southeast Asia.


According to


[IDC's How Southeast Asia Buys and Pays 2025](https://paymentsindustryintelligence.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/How-Southeast-Asia-Buys-and-Pays.pdf) ,


**offline methods** such as cash on delivery and ATM transfers made up 13% of the region's e-commerce payments in 2023, and that share is


**projected to fall to 6% by 2028** . If your business plans to expand into Southeast Asia, this shift means


**preparing the digital payment options** that customers in each market prefer.


Those


**preferences** differ from market to market, and no single payment method accounts for most of the region's e-commerce payment value:


- In 2023, cards were the largest payment method by value at US$40.8 billion, ahead of domestic payments at US$38.9 billion and mobile wallets at US$35.4 billion (Domestic payments refer to real-time payments and local bank-based payment schemes).


- **By 2028** ,


**domestic payments** are projected to reach US$97.9 billion,


**mobile wallets** US$94.9 billion, and


**cards** US$93.9 billion. Domestic payments and mobile wallets are projected to grow faster because they help e-commerce reach more customers in a region that has traditionally relied less on cards.


With domestic payments, mobile wallets, and cards projected to carry almost the same payment value by 2028, your business


**cannot rely on one payment method** to reach customers across the region. A checkout built mainly around cards would focus on a method projected to drop from the largest to the third largest by value.


The differences run deeper than consumer habits. Each country has built a


[national instant payment system to unify domestic payments](https://www.imf.org/-/media/files/publications/fandd/article/2025/09/freischlad.pdf) under its own standard:


- **Singapore (**[PayNow](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/payment-channel-page-push-14) **)** Introduced by Singapore's banking association in 2017, PayNow lets people send money in real time using a mobile number or national ID, and lets businesses receive payments using their unique entity number.


- **Malaysia (**[DuitNow](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/duitnow-pay) **) and Thailand (**[PromptPay](https://www.xendit.co/en-th/blog/accepting-mobile-banking-payments-in-thailand-a-complete-guide-for-businesses/) **)** Both systems follow an approach similar to Singapore's, supporting instant transfers to a mobile number or ID in the style of India's Unified Payments Interface (UPI).
******


- **Indonesia (**[QRIS](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/qris) **and BI-FAST)** Indonesia introduced BI-FAST, Bank Indonesia's real-time transfer system, and QRIS, the national QR code standard that Bank Indonesia and the country's payment association established in 2019.


These national systems were built mainly for domestic use, so a local payment method usually serves customers within its own country. For example, QRIS transactions remain mostly domestic, and a customer using a mobile wallet from outside Indonesia would likely be unable to pay with a QRIS code.


***Also read:***[QR Payments in Malaysia: A Business Guide to Accepting DuitNow](https://www.xendit.co/en-my/blog/qr-payments-in-malaysia-a-business-guide-to-accepting-duitnow/)


### **A payment mix that works in one market may not work in another**


Because each country has its own national payment system and preferred payment methods, a business entering Indonesia cannot assume that the methods performing well in Singapore will produce the same results. A checkout built for Singapore around PayNow and cards would leave out the QR payments, local e-wallets, and bank virtual accounts that many Indonesian customers use online. A virtual account assigns each order its own bank account number for the customer to transfer to.


Offering many payment methods across the region does not guarantee coverage in each market, since a checkout can support a long list of methods and still miss the two or three that most customers in one country use. What determines conversion in each market is whether your business supports the payment methods customers there prefer, so each market needs its own payment mix, based on local payment behavior and your own conversion data.


***Also read:***[E-Commerce Payment Strategy in Southeast Asia: Winning on Conversion, Reliability, and Scale](https://www.xendit.co/en/blog/e-commerce-payment-strategy-in-southeast-asia-winning-on-conversion-reliability-and-scale/)


### **Localization affects more than the checkout page**


Supporting a local payment method also changes what happens around the payment itself.


**Payment localization** can


**affect** four parts of each transaction:


- **How payment options are presented** Some payment methods redirect the customer to a bank or e-wallet app to approve the payment, while others show a QR code or payment code that the customer completes in a separate app. Your checkout has to handle each of these flows correctly, since a customer who gets stuck between your site and a payment app can easily abandon the order.


- **How transactions are processed** Each payment method sets its own minimum and maximum amounts, and its own time limit before an unpaid payment request expires. If an order is above a method's maximum amount, the customer cannot pay with that method, and if the payment request expires before the customer pays, the order stays unpaid. Your checkout needs to show the methods that fit each order value and make the payment deadline clear to the customer.


- **How payments are confirmed** Most methods confirm within minutes, while some bank transfer methods can take up to a business day, which affects when your team can release an order. Your order system needs to wait for confirmation before releasing goods, and your customer service team needs to know which methods confirm later, so a pending payment is not treated as a failed one.
- **How refunds and settlements are handled**[Refund support and refund windows differ by method](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/refund-payment-request) , and[settlement](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/settlements-overview) can arrive almost instantly on some real-time rails or take several business days on cards. Your returns policy has to match what each method allows, and your finance team has to plan cash flow around settlement dates that differ from one method to another.Each of these four differences is manageable within a single market. As your business adds more markets, they multiply into **separate processes** that your teams have to learn, track, and support for each market. Keeping them under control depends on the payment infrastructure behind your checkout, which should stay **standardized** across markets.


## **Standardization: Keeping regional expansion manageable with one payment infrastructure**


While the payment methods customers see should follow each market, the payment infrastructure behind them should stay the same across markets. Standardizing your payment infrastructure matters for three reasons:


### **Separate payment integrations for each market create unnecessary complexity**


When every market requires its own payment integration,


**regional expansion** adds


**technical dependencies** with each country. Each market added through a separate payment integration can bring another:


- Payment provider connection


- API integration to build and maintain


- Set of transaction flows and status codes


- Operational workflow for the teams that handle payment issues


The payment stack becomes harder to maintain with each addition, and your engineering team spends a growing share of its time keeping existing connections running instead of building the product.


***Also read:***[Scaling E-Commerce Payments Across Southeast Asia: Why Businesses Need Cross-Border Payment Infrastructure](https://www.xendit.co/en/blog/scaling-e-commerce-payments-across-southeast-asia-why-businesses-need-cross-border-payment-infrastructure/)


### **Finance and operations need consistent data**


Separate payment setups create extra work for finance and operations teams as well. When each market runs through a different payment provider, these teams end up working with different versions of the same information:


- Transaction reports in different formats


- Payment statuses that each provider defines differently


- Refund processes with separate steps and timelines


- Settlement data that arrives on different schedules


- Reconciliation workflows rebuilt for each market


Even small differences between providers add


**manual work** for your finance team. For example, if one provider reports transaction times in local time and another in UTC, a transaction can look


**missing during reconciliation** simply because the timestamps do not line up. A customer may pay with a localized method, but your finance team should not have to run a different system every time a new market goes live.


### **Standardization creates a consistent operating layer**


A standardized layer gives every market the


**same operating foundation** , even when the payment methods on top of it differ. Ideally, a standardized payment infrastructure allows your business to:


- Connect to different local payment methods through one integration


- Manage transactions with the same statuses and data fields in every market


- Monitor payment activity across countries from one place


- Handle refunds and settlements through a common workflow


Southeast Asia's central banks are applying the same principle to their national payment systems, keeping each country's system and standardizing how the systems connect. The first


**bilateral link** between


**two national systems** connected Singapore's PayNow and Thailand's PromptPay in 2021, and it took


[three years of collaboration to finalize](https://www.imf.org/-/media/files/publications/fandd/article/2025/09/freischlad.pdf) . Each link needs its own


**technical alignment** , plus


**alignment of domestic rules on data privacy** ,


**security** , and


**sanctions screening** . To avoid repeating that effort for every pair of countries, several central banks established


[Nexus Global Payments](https://nexusglobalpayments.org/about-nexus/) in April 2025. Through its Nexus gateway, each national system connects once, under


**common technical and operating standards** , to reach every other country in the network, and the first live transaction is expected around


**2027** .


Your business can follow the same design by keeping each market's local payment methods and standardizing the payment infrastructure that connects them to your systems and teams.


Localization and standardization are both necessary but they need balance, as problems start when a business leans too far toward one of them.


## **Finding the right balance between localization and standardization**


For payments, localization and standardization are both necessary, and each one belongs to a different layer. Localization covers the payment experience customers see, while standardization covers the payment infrastructure your teams operate.


Standardization works best when customer preferences are similar across markets, and payment preferences in Southeast Asia differ widely from one country to the next. Even companies known for standardization, such as Apple, adapt payment methods to regional preferences, which makes payment methods one of the first things to localize.


Leaning too far toward either approach creates problems of its own:


### **Over-standardizing**


A business may try to


**run exactly the same payment setup in every market** . This approach can lead to:


- **Payment methods customers rarely use** , because the default payment method mix reflects the default market


- **Lower relevance at checkout** , since the payment options on screen do not match how customers in that market usually pay


- **Missed payment opportunities** , when customers leave without completing the order because their preferred payment method is not available


- **A checkout that feels disconnected from the local market** , which weakens trust at the moment a customer decides whether to pay


These losses rarely appear as payment problems in your data. They tend to look like weak demand in a new market, when the actual cause is a missing payment method.


### **Over-localizing**


A business can also go in the opposite direction and


**build a separate payment setup for every market** . This approach can lead to:


- **Multiple payment integrations** to build, test, and update whenever a provider releases changes


- **Fragmented transaction data** , with no single place to see payment volume or performance across markets


- **More operational work** , as support teams learn a different provider process for each country


- **More complicated reconciliation** , since the month-end close waits on the slowest provider's report


- **Higher maintenance requirements** , including separate contracts, vendor reviews, and compliance checks for each provider


- **Greater complexity when entering another market** , because each new country starts with a new build


Localization is also considerably more expensive, more resource-intensive, and harder to scale than standardization. In payments, that cost keeps growing, because each separate setup adds maintenance, reporting, and reconciliation work for as long as the market stays live.


Both approaches answer different questions, so it helps to compare them side by side before deciding where each one belongs in your payment setup:


**Localization**


**Standardization**


**What it applies to** Payment acceptance at checkout in each market


The infrastructure that processes, records, and settles those payments


**What it covers** Payment methods, approval flow, currency shown, payment instructions


Integration, payment statuses and notifications, refunds, reporting, reconciliation


**Who experiences it** Customers in each country


Your engineering, finance, and operations teams


**What it delivers** A checkout that matches how customers in that market already pay


One way of working that stays the same in every market


**What it costs when overdone** Separate setups per market, fragmented transaction data, higher maintenance


Payment methods few customers use, weaker checkout relevance, lost orders


**What happens when you add a market** Adjusted per market, based on local payment behavior


Stays the same, extended through configuration


###


### **The better balance**


**Localize the payment acceptance** , and


**standardize the infrastructure** that operates it. Your customers get a payment experience that fits their market, while your business keeps one consistent way to integrate, monitor, reconcile, and manage those payments. In practice, the split between the two layers looks like this:


- **Localize:** The payment methods in each market, the approval flow each method needs, the currency customers see, and the payment instructions they follow


- **Standardize:** The integration, payment statuses and notifications, the refund workflow, reporting, and reconciliation


Maintaining this balance as your business adds markets depends on the payment infrastructure you choose.

## **What scalable regional payment infrastructure should provide**


Before expanding into a new market or redesigning its payment setup, a business should


**evaluate** its


**regional payment infrastructure** in five areas:


- **Local payment coverage** The first question is whether the infrastructure supports the payment methods customers actually use in each target market. Check coverage market by market and method by method, since a long regional total can still miss the two or three methods that carry most payments in a specific country. Review the


[features each payment channel supports](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/available-payment-channels) as well, such as refunds, saved payment details, and installments.


The second question is how a new payment method gets added. When adding a local method means


[activating a payment channel](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/activate-payment-channels) on an existing account, your business can respond to local demand without replacing its payment setup.


- **A consistent integration layer** Next, check whether multiple payment methods connect through a common integration, and whether your business can enter another market without building a separate technical architecture. In a common integration, every payment method uses the


[same request structure and the same set of responses](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/how-payments-api-work) , so adding a method or a market extends the existing build. A simple test is whether adding the tenth payment method takes less development work than adding the first.


Payment confirmation should work the same way for every method as well. A consistent webhook, the automated message your system receives when a payment status changes, lets your order system handle a QR payment in Thailand and an e-wallet payment in the Philippines with the same logic.
- **Consistent payment operations** Operations stay manageable when every payment follows the same lifecycle from confirmation to refund and settlement, whatever method the customer used. The question for finance and operations teams is whether they can manage transaction status, refunds, settlements, and reconciliation through one workflow.Reconciliation deserves a closer look.[Transaction reconciliation](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/reconciliations) links each order in your system to its payment, while bank reconciliation matches payment records to the funds that reach your bank account. Both get harder when each provider formats its records differently, and simpler when every payment record follows one structure.
- **Cross-market visibility** Your teams should be able to monitor payment activity across countries and methods in one place, then narrow it down by market, method, or status when a problem appears. For finance, the test is whether payment information arrives in[one consistent format](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/reports-overview) . When each provider exports its own file, someone on your team has to combine and reformat those files before reconciliation can start, and that work grows with every market added.


- **Regional scalability** Finally, check whether the infrastructure can take on new markets, new payment methods, and higher transaction volumes without multiplying operational complexity. Regulatory coverage belongs in the same check. A payment provider needs the relevant[license](https://www.xendit.co/en/company/xendit-licenses/) in each market where it offers regulated payment services, and those licenses determine whether local collection and settlement can run under each country's rules once your business goes live.


***Also read:***[What to Look for in a Payment Partner When Expanding from the US to Asia](https://www.xendit.co/en/blog/what-to-look-for-payment-partner-expanding-us-to-southeast-asia/)


These five areas are what a payment infrastructure needs to support your business as it grows across Southeast Asia.


## **How Xendit combines localized payment acceptance with standardized payment operations**


Xendit provides one payment infrastructure for Southeast Asia, so your business can offer local payment methods in each country while


**integration** ,


**operations** , and


**reporting** run through the same setup.


These are the


**five Xendit capabilities that support localized payment acceptance and standardized payment operations** as your business expands across the region:


## **1. Local payment acceptance through one integration**


Xendit enables your business to accept


[100+ payment methods](https://www.xendit.co/en/products/all-payment-methods/) across Southeast Asia through


**a single integration** , covering local payment methods alongside international cards. Your payment mix can follow each market, from national QR and real-time methods such as QRIS in Indonesia, PromptPay in Thailand, DuitNow in Malaysia, and PayNow in Singapore, to e-wallets such as GCash and Maya in the Philippines and MoMo and ZaloPay in Vietnam, without building each connection independently.


You can choose how to integrate with Xendit based on how your online store is built. If your store runs on Shopify or WooCommerce, you can connect through Xendit's


[plug-ins](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/how-plug-ins-work) . If your business runs its own website on a custom-built system, you can use the


[Payments API](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/how-payments-api-work) or add Xendit's checkout components through


[Payment Sessions](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/how-payment-sessions-work) . On the API, every method runs through the same payment request endpoint, and Xendit returns the next step your checkout should show the customer, such as a redirect to an e-wallet app or a QR code to scan. Simple use cases can go live in a few weeks and more complex ones in up to a month, with less development work for each payment method you add after that.


Localization can extend to currency as well. With


[card multi-currency processing](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/card-multi-currency-processing) , shoppers may pay by card in their own currency while your business settles in one currency, and Xendit's reports show the charged amount, converted amount, and FX rate for each transaction. International cardholders see a familiar amount at checkout, and your finance team receives funds in a predictable currency. The feature is rolling out country by country, starting with Hong Kong, Singapore, and Thailand.


### **2. A centralized view across entities and operations**


With


[XenPlatform](https://www.xendit.co/en/products/xenplatform/) , your business can manage and view transactions across its branches, subsidiaries, or business units from a single dashboard. Each entity runs as a


[sub-account](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/sub-accounts) with its own balance and transaction history, while the head office sees every sub-account, its status, and its cash balance in one


[Accounts Overview](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/xenplatform-monitoring-transactions) . Finance teams can


[export consolidated balance or transaction reports](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/consolidated-reports) for selected sub-accounts, and


[transfers](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/transfer-balances) move balances from subsidiary accounts to the main account when funds are needed centrally.


For a group with separate entities in several markets, this keeps each entity's records separate for accounting while the regional team works from one view of payment activity.


### **3. Cross-border payouts and FX capabilities**


Regional growth also means sending money outward and across currencies. Xendit supports payouts to 180+ countries, with


[cross-border payments](https://www.xendit.co/en/products/cross-border-payments/) that convert major and varied currencies at wholesale rates, so your business can pay suppliers, partners, and group entities without adding a provider for each destination. In markets including Indonesia, the Philippines, Malaysia, Thailand, Vietnam, and Singapore, Xendit sends local payouts through


[direct integrations with local clearing systems](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/overview-payouts-coverage) , making it faster and more cost-effective than SWIFT transfers.


On the collection side, funds can settle in the country where they were collected or to your central entity, subject to eligibility and each country's regulatory requirements. Your treasury team can then keep funds where the business needs them, instead of where each payment happened to be collected.


***Also read:***[Multi-Currency FX and Settlement in Southeast Asia: A Guide for Regional Finance Teams](https://www.xendit.co/en/blog/multi-currency-fx-and-settlement-in-southeast-asia-a-guide-for-regional-finance-teams/)


### **4. Infrastructure supported by local licenses**


Xendit’s regulated payment services run under licenses held by entities within the Xendit group.


[The licenses](https://www.xendit.co/en/company/xendit-licenses/) for Southeast Asia include:


- **Indonesia:** Payment Gateway license (Category 1) from Bank Indonesia


- **Philippines:** Operator of Payment System from Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas


- **Singapore:** Major Payment Institution license from the Monetary Authority of Singapore


- **Malaysia:** Merchant Acquiring Services from Bank Negara Malaysia


- **Thailand:** Payment Service Provider and Electronic Money Service Provider licenses from the Bank of Thailand


- **Vietnam:** Payment Intermediary Services from the State Bank of Vietnam


For your legal and procurement teams, this means one partner to assess across markets, with no separate licensing review for each local provider, and payment services in each country running under that country's regulatory requirements.


### **5. Consistent payment operations**


The operating layer stays the same across every method and market. Xendit confirms payments through


[webhook notifications](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/handling-webhooks) , and every transaction carries the same pair of


[transaction and settlement statuses](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/transaction-status) across the dashboard, API responses, and reports.


[Refund requests](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/refund-payment-request) reference the original payment request and return a refund.succeeded or refund.failed webhook, so your systems track refunds the same way in every market.


For finance, the


[transactions report](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/transactions-report) lists payments from every market with the same columns, including fees, net amount, settlement status, and estimated settlement date. It can be downloaded on demand,


[scheduled for delivery](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/scheduling-reports) to email or an SFTP server, or generated through the API, so reconciliation data reaches your finance systems without manual assembly.


Together, these capabilities let your business adapt checkout to each market while every payment runs through the same operating layer.


### **Build a Southeast Asia payment strategy that scales across markets**


Expanding across Southeast Asia calls for both localization and standardization, each applied to a different layer of your payment setup. Localize what customers see and use at checkout, and standardize how payments are integrated and operated underneath.


Localized payment acceptance can run on one shared infrastructure across every country you serve. With that infrastructure in place, adding a local payment method or entering another market extends the setup you already run, and your teams avoid creating another fragmented payment system to maintain.

## **FAQ for businesses expanding across Southeast Asia: Localizing and standardizing payments**


### **Should I use a local payment provider in each Southeast Asian country or one regional provider?**


A local provider in each country can give you depth in that one market, but each one adds its own integration, contract, report format, and reconciliation process. A regional provider can cover local methods across markets through one integration, as long as it holds the licenses each market requires.


**Xendit** gives your business access to


[local payment methods](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/available-payment-channels) across Southeast Asia from a single account, backed by licenses held by Xendit group entities in each market.


### **Can I add a local payment method in one country without changing my checkout in other markets?**


Yes, as long as your markets share one integration. With


**Xendit** , you activate a new payment channel from the dashboard, and depending on the channel, it becomes available instantly after account verification, by request in the dashboard, or through


[Xendit's support team](https://www.xendit.co/en/contact/contact-sales) . On the


[Payments API](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/how-payments-api-work) , the new channel uses the same payment request as your existing methods with a different channel code, so the checkout flows already live in your other markets will stay as they are.


### **Can a company without a local entity accept local payment methods in Southeast Asia?**


In many cases, yes, though availability depends on the market and the payment method.


**Xendit** publishes


[verification requirements](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/singapore-and-others-business-documents) for businesses incorporated outside Southeast Asia and lists which payment channels each business entity type can


[activate](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/activate-payment-channels) . E-wallet, bank transfer, QR, and international card payments


[can be accepted across](https://www.xendit.co/en/blog/what-to-look-for-payment-partner-expanding-us-to-southeast-asia/) Xendit’s Southeast Asian markets without a local entity, while domestic card processing requires one, so confirm the channels for each target market with


[Xendit's team](https://www.xendit.co/en/contact/contact-sales) before planning a launch.


### **Why do refund rules differ between payment methods in Southeast Asia?**


Refund support is set by each payment channel, so the options change from


[method to method](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/available-payment-channels) . GCash in the Philippines supports full and partial refunds for up to 180 days, QRIS in Indonesia supports full refunds for up to 30 days, and PromptPay in Thailand does not support refunds through the original payment route.


**Xendit** returns supported refunds to the customer's original payment method, and for channels without refund support,


[Payout Links](https://www.xendit.co/en/products/xenpayout/) let your team send the money back without collecting the customer's account details first.


### **How do I reconcile payments from different local payment methods in one process?**


Pass your own order ID as the reference ID on every payment request, whatever the method, so each


**Xendit** record can be matched to an order in your system. Xendit's


[Transactions Report](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/transactions-report) labels each payment with a channel category, such as e-wallet, QR code, virtual account, direct debit, or card, so your team can filter and review each group from the same export. Set a timezone rule early as well, since reports generated through the API use UTC while dashboard exports use the timezone of the user who exports them.
